title: Why Art Matters: The Power of Stories in Human Life
paragraphs: In every known human culture, people tell stories. Cave paintings, oral epics, religious parables, novels, films, and video games are all variations on the same fundamental impulse: to represent human experience in a form that can be shared, examined, and passed on. This universality suggests that storytelling is not merely entertainment — it is a core cognitive and social function, as essential to human life as language itself.

Psychologists and neuroscientists have begun to map what happens in the brain when we engage with narrative art. Studies using fMRI scanning have shown that reading fiction activates not just the language centres of the brain, but also the regions associated with actual physical experience, emotional processing, and social cognition. When we read that a character is cold and afraid, our brains simulate the experience of being cold and afraid. This is not metaphorical immersion — it is neurological. The brain, to a significant extent, cannot fully distinguish between experiencing something and vividly imagining it.

This neurological reality has significant implications. Reading fiction, watching films, and engaging with drama expose us to the inner lives of people whose circumstances, backgrounds, and worldviews are radically different from our own. Research by psychologists Keith Oatley and Raymond Mar found that people who read fiction extensively score higher on measures of empathy and social understanding than people who read primarily non-fiction. The mechanism seems to be "theory of mind" — the cognitive ability to model other people's mental states — which is exercised and developed by the practice of inhabiting fictional perspectives.

Beyond empathy, great art offers something else: a vocabulary for experiences that might otherwise be inarticulate. Reading a poem about grief that captures something you have felt but never been able to express can be transformative — not because the poem teaches you something new, but because it names something you already know. Philosopher Martha Nussbaum has argued that literary imagination is essential to moral reasoning: the ability to imagine other people's lives fully and specifically, to understand why they feel what they feel and choose what they choose, is necessary for genuine ethical thought.

The power of art to challenge assumptions and reshape consciousness is also a reason why it has so often been feared and suppressed. Authoritarian regimes throughout history have understood that controlling the stories a society tells is a powerful form of political control. Books are banned and burned not because they are lies, but because they might tell a kind of truth that those in power find dangerous. The arts, at their best, hold up a mirror to society — and not everyone likes what they see.

Film has become the most widely consumed art form of the modern era. A significant proportion of what people know about other countries, other historical periods, and other ways of life comes not from direct experience or academic study, but from cinema. This gives filmmakers an enormous responsibility — and an enormous opportunity. A film can reach millions of people who would never read a history book, never visit a particular country, and never encounter a person from a particular background. When it does so with honesty and depth, it can change how those millions think, feel, and act.

None of this means that art must be didactic — that it must teach lessons or deliver moral messages. The greatest works of art are often morally complex, formally experimental, or emotionally ambiguous. They resist easy interpretation precisely because reality itself resists easy interpretation. What they offer is not answers, but the experience of asking better questions — the experience of sitting with complexity, uncertainty, and humanity long enough to come away more alive to it.
